summary: A landlocked country in the South Caucasus; in 301 CE it became the first country in the world to adopt Christianity as its state religion, and it has a distinctive script and a long-standing culture.

ranking.name: Armenian Apostolic Church
ranking.description: According to tradition, in 301 CE King Tiridates III was converted by Saint Gregory the Illuminator and baptized, making Armenia the first country in the world to adopt Christianity as its state religion. In 451 the Armenian Church did not attend, or did not accept, the decisions of the Council of Chalcedon, and from then on became an independent Oriental Orthodox church; through the thousand years in which Armenia was ruled by Persia, the Arabs, the Ottomans and Russia, the Church has always been at the core of national identity, which is why more than 90 percent are believers.

ranking.name: Other Christians (Catholics, Protestants, etc.)
ranking.description: Catholics are mainly Armenian Catholics, mostly found in the Shirak region of the north, some of whom are descendants of residents who moved from the Ottoman Empire after the Russo-Turkish war of the early 19th century. Protestantism appeared under the influence of American Congregationalist missionaries in the 19th century, and after independence in 1991 Evangelicals and Pentecostals also grew, but overall they remain a minority.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: During the Soviet period (1920-1991) atheism was promoted, churches were closed, the clergy were suppressed, and religious education was cut off. But because the Armenian Church is closely tied to national identity, after independence the great majority of people again identified with the Church, and those who identify as having no religion make up only a very small share.

ranking.name: Yazidism and other religions
ranking.description: Yazidism is the ancient religion of the Yazidis, a Kurdish-speaking people, blending ancient Iranian beliefs with Islamic Sufi elements. From the 19th to the early 20th century, many Yazidis fled persecution by the Ottoman Empire and moved, together with Armenians, to the Russian-ruled Armenian region; they live mainly in Aragatsotn and Armavir provinces, and in 2019 the world's largest Yazidi temple was completed there.

religion.background: Before Christianity, Armenia followed a polytheistic faith with Aramazd as chief god and was influenced by Zoroastrianism. Christianity became the state religion in 301, and around 405 Mesrop Mashtots created the Armenian alphabet in order to translate the Bible; religion and script together shaped the national culture. After that Armenia long lay among great powers such as Persia, Byzantium, the Arabs and the Ottomans, and when the state perished the Church took the place of the government in holding the people together. The Armenian Genocide by the Ottoman Empire in 1915 and religious oppression in the Soviet period both severely damaged the Church, and after independence in 1991 the Church again became the center of national life.

ranking.name: Armenian
ranking.description: Armenian is an independent branch of the Indo-European family; around 405 Mesrop Mashtots created 36 letters, giving it a written history of more than 1,600 years. In modern times it is divided into Eastern Armenian and Western Armenian, and the Republic of Armenia uses Eastern Armenian. The 1915 genocide and the post-war population exchanges made Armenia a country with a highly homogeneous ethnic composition, so 97 percent of the population speak it as their mother tongue.

ranking.name: Russian
ranking.description: Russian entered Armenia after Russia took the Yerevan region from Persia in 1828, and in the Soviet period it was the main language of administration, science and higher education. After independence in 1991 Russian lost its official status and has few native speakers, but many people still use it as a second language, and economic exchanges with Russia and the wave of migrant labor have kept Russian in use.

ranking.name: Yazidi (Kurdish)
ranking.description: Yazidi is a form of the northern Kurdish dialect (Kurmanji), spoken by the Yazidis, most of whom fled from the eastern Ottoman Empire to Armenia between the 19th and early 20th centuries. In the Soviet 1930s a Kurdish-language newspaper and radio broadcasts were published in Yerevan, and Armenia remains an important place for preserving Yazidi language culture.

language.history: The earliest documents in Armenian appeared after the creation of the alphabet in 405, and the 5th century is called the 'Golden Age' of Armenian literature, when a large number of religious and historical works were translated or written; this classical language is called 'Grabar'. After the Middle Ages the spoken language gradually diverged, and in the 19th century two modern standard languages, Eastern and Western, formed, centered on the Yerevan area and Constantinople respectively. The 1915 genocide scattered speakers of Western Armenian around the world, and today it survives mainly in overseas diaspora communities. After independence in 1991, Eastern Armenian became the sole official language.

ranking.name: Khorovats
ranking.description: Pieces of pork, lamb or chicken are marinated, threaded onto long iron skewers and grilled over charcoal, usually served with grilled vegetables, onions and lavash flatbread.
ranking.history: Armenians regard grilled meat as an important social and festive food, and it is almost indispensable at weekend outings, weddings and family gatherings. Because Armenia is a Christian country, pork khorovats is especially popular, which differs from the lamb skewers of the neighboring Islamic countries. In the Soviet period it also became popular across the Caucasus and was called 'shashlik' by the Russians, but Armenians insist on using the local name 'khorovats'.

ranking.name: Dolma
ranking.description: Grape leaves or cabbage leaves are wrapped around ground meat, rice and herbs, or the filling is stuffed into eggplants, green peppers and tomatoes and stewed, often served with garlic yogurt.
ranking.history: Leaf-wrapped dishes have a long history in the Caucasus, Iran and the Ottoman region, and Armenia, Azerbaijan and Turkey each regard it as their own tradition, so the name and origin often cause disputes. Armenian grape growing goes back thousands of years, and grape leaves are a product of one's own vineyard; during Lent, believers make a vegetarian version filled with beans and rice. Every year some places also hold a dolma festival to celebrate the dish.

ranking.name: Lavash
ranking.description: Dough of flour, water and salt is rolled into very thin large sheets and stuck to the wall of a clay oven, the 'tonir', to bake; it is soft and can be rolled around other food.
ranking.history: Lavash has a history of thousands of years in Armenia; traditionally it was made collectively by village women in a tonir, and after drying it keeps for months and returns to softness when dampened, suiting mountain life. At weddings lavash is draped over the shoulders of the couple, symbolizing abundance and good luck. In 2014 UNESCO inscribed 'Lavash, the preparation, meaning and appearance of traditional bread as an expression of culture in Armenia' on its list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

ranking.name: Khash
ranking.description: Cow or sheep trotters are boiled for a long time into a light, thick soup, which is served with a great deal of crushed garlic and salt and eaten with dried lavash.
ranking.history: Khash was originally a cheap dish that farmers made from the cow's feet left over after slaughtering, and it is already recorded in medieval documents. Traditionally it is a winter food, eaten with friends on cold early mornings together with vodka or mulberry spirit. Armenians treat eating khash as a ritual, and there is a saying that it is eaten only in months with the letter R in the name (that is, the autumn and winter months).

ranking.name: Ghapama
ranking.description: A hollowed-out pumpkin is filled with rice, raisins, dried apricots, nuts and honey and baked whole; it is cut open when served, sweet, fragrant and tender.
ranking.history: Ghapama is a sweet dish of Armenian winter and festivals, often appearing during New Year and Christmas (which the Armenian Church celebrates on 6 January). It uses pumpkins harvested in autumn and homemade sun-dried fruit, reflecting the agricultural products of the Armenian highlands. The folk song 'Hey Jan Ghapama' even describes the scene of a whole family gathering around ghapama to celebrate, making it a symbol of family reunion.
